title.en: The golden-armed leader, and the lord of the quarters, the paths and the fields

summary: Thirteen yajus, each opening and closing with namaḥ. Rudra is saluted in the forms Sāyaṇa calls his forms taken in play for sustaining the world: the golden-armed leader of armies, the green-haired trees, the charioteer, the counsellor and the merchant, the loud-crying warrior. Each yajus also salutes him as the lord (pati) — for Sāyaṇa, the protector (पालक) — of the quarters, animals, paths, foods, fields, forests, trees, thickets, plants, foot-soldiers and warriors.

samasa.vigraha: हिरण्यनिर्मितानि आभरणानि बाह्वोः यस्य सः हिरण्यबाहुः
samasa.meaning: he whose arms [bear ornaments] of gold; golden-armed (the vigraha is Sāyaṇa’s)
leader of an army (-nī from √nī, ‘to lead’)

vyakarana.note: Each yajus of this anuvāka begins and ends with namaḥ (Sāyaṇa: «नमस्कारादिकं नमस्कारान्तम् एकैकं यजुः»). The verb is understood: ‘homage [be]’. Every dative of the yajus depends on it (namaḥ takes the dative, P. 2.3.16).
Dative singular of the root noun senānī: the final ī of -nī becomes y before the vowel of the ending (senānī + e → senānye).

Dative of pati with the regular i-stem ending. In Classical Sanskrit uncompounded pati has patye (P. 1.4.8, patiḥ samāsa eva); in the Veda pati construed with a genitive may take the ordinary forms (P. 1.4.9, ṣaṣṭhīyuktaś chandasi vā) — so diśām … pataye, ‘to the lord of the quarters’, and the same in every yajus of this anuvāka.

translation.literal: Homage to the golden-armed, to the leader of the army, and to the lord of the quarters homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the golden-armed leader of armies; homage to the lord of the quarters.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa begins by placing the anuvāka: the first anuvāka appeased Rudra’s principal form, and the next eight appease the forms he takes in play that sustain the world («लीला-विग्रहा जगन्-निर्वाह-हेतवस्»). All of them are yajus; in three of these anuvākas each yajus begins and ends with a namaskāra («नमस्कारादिकं नमस्कारान्तम् एकैकं यजुः»), and this anuvāka has thirteen («द्वितीयेऽनुवाके त्रयोदश यजूंषि»). On the first: hiraṇyabāhu is he on whose arms are ornaments made of gold («हिरण्यनिर्मितान्याभरणानि बाह्वोर्यस्य»), and senānī he who leads the army in battles («संग्रामेषु सेनां नयतीति सेनानीः»); homage is to the Rudra who bears such a form («तादृशमूर्तिधरो यो रुद्रस्तस्मै नमोऽस्तु»). The lord of the quarters is the Rudra who protects the directions («यश्च दिशां पालको रुद्रस्तस्मै नमोऽस्तु»).
units.reflection: The same Rudra who was feared in the first anuvāka is now met as a leader and a guardian of every direction; homage moves from facing a weapon to recognising an order.

vyakarana.note: An adjective agreeing with vṛkṣebhyaḥ (dative plural). hari is the colour between yellow and green; here, of leaves, green.
Genitive plural of the u-stem paśu, dependent on pataye: ‘the lord of the animals’ (in the Veda pati with a genitive keeps the ordinary dative pataye; see yajus 1).

translation.literal: Homage to the trees, the green-haired; to the lord of the animals homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the trees with their green hair; homage to the lord of the animals.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: the trees are green-haired because their leaves are their hair («हरितवर्णाः केशाः पर्णरूपा येषां वृक्षाणां ते हरिकेशाः»), and the homage is to such trees as forms of Rudra in the shape of trees («वृक्षाकाररुद्रमूर्तिभ्यः»). The lord of the animals is the Rudra who protects them («यो रुद्रः पशूनां पालकः»).

samasa.meaning: tawny like young grass; one syllable pi is lost in the joining, which Sāyaṇa justifies as a form of the pṛṣodara class (P. 6.3.109)

vyakarana.note: saspi ‘young grass’ + piñjara ‘tawny, reddish-yellow’, with one pi dropped (saspi-piñjara → saspiñjara): an irregular formation accepted as found (pṛṣodarādi, P. 6.3.109), as Sāyaṇa says. Monier-Williams records the word as the Taittirīya spelling of śaṣpiñjara (from śaṣpa, ‘young grass’).
tviṣi ‘brilliance, vehemence’ + the possessive suffix -mat, with the i lengthened before the suffix (tviṣī-mat), a Vedic form; dative singular -mate.
Vedic genitive plural of path- ‘path’ (Monier-Williams cites pathīnām from the Ṛgveda and Atharvaveda); the Classical form is पथाम्. Not to be normalised.

translation.literal: Homage to the one tawny like young grass, to the brilliant one; to the lord of the paths homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the radiant one, tawny as young grass; homage to the lord of the paths.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: saspi denotes young grass («सस्पिं-शब्दो बालतृणवाची») and piñjara a colour of mixed yellow and red («पीतरक्तसंकीर्णवर्णवाची पिञ्जरः»); saspiñjara, ‘tawny like young grass’, is a correct form as one of the pṛṣodara class. tviṣīmat is दीप्तिमान्, radiant; homage is to the form of Rudra that is so. The paths are those taught in the śāstra, the southern, the northern and the third («शास्त्रोक्तदक्षिणोत्तरतृतीयमार्गाणां»), and their lord is the Rudra who protects them.

flags.note: pathīnām is literally ‘of the paths, roads’; Sāyaṇa specifies them as the southern, northern and third paths of the śāstra. The translation keeps ‘paths’ and the traditional note gives his reading.

samasa.meaning: he who rests on the bull (babhlu = babhru, ‘the bearer’, the bull); Sāyaṇa’s analysis

vyakarana.note: Sāyaṇa derives babhru from bhṛ, ‘to carry’ (the bull carries Rudra), takes babhlu as the same word with l for r («रलयोर्भेदाभावः»), and -śa from śī, ‘to lie, rest’. Monier-Williams gives the word simply as ‘brownish’ (from babhru, ‘brown’).
vi-vyādhin, ‘piercing through’: vi + √vyadh + the agent suffix -in (one who habitually does so); dative singular -ine.
Genitive plural of the a-stem anna, ‘food’; the a after vivyādhine is elided (avagraha in the text: विव्याधिनेऽन्नानाम्).

translation.literal: Homage to the one resting on the bull, to the piercing one; to the lord of foods homage.
translation.readable: Homage to him who rides the bull and pierces through; homage to the lord of foods.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: the bull is called babhru because it carries Rudra («बभ्रुर्वृषभः»); babhlu is the same word, r and l not being distinguished («रलयोर्भेदाभावः»), and babhluśa is he who rests on it. vivyādhin is he who pierces his enemies especially («विद्वेषिणो विशेषेण विध्यतीति विव्याधी»). The lord of foods is the Rudra who protects them («यश्चान्नानां पालको रुद्रस्तस्मै नमोऽस्तु»).

flags.note: babhluśa: Monier-Williams ‘brownish’ (a colour word, from babhru ‘brown’); Sāyaṇa ‘he who rests on the bull’. The translation follows Sāyaṇa; the word table gives both.

vyakarana.note: upavīta, the cord worn over the left shoulder (from upa-√vye, ‘to wrap’), + the possessive suffix -in: ‘having the cord on’; dative singular -ine.
Past participle of √puṣ, ‘to thrive, be nourished’, used as a noun, genitive plural. The form is the same in the masculine and the neuter; Sāyaṇa takes it as masculine (persons).

translation.literal: Homage to the dark-haired one, to the one wearing the sacred cord; to the lord of those who thrive homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the dark-haired one who wears the sacred cord; homage to the lord of those who thrive.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: harikeśa is dark-haired and free of grey hair («पलितरहिताय»), and upavītin is the Rudra who wears the sacrificial cord for auspiciousness («मङ्गलार्थं यज्ञोपवीतधारिणे रुद्राय नमोऽस्तु»). The puṣṭa are men full in good qualities («परिपूर्णगुणानां पुरुषाणां»), and pati here is their master («पतये स्वामिने नमोऽस्तु»).

flags.note: hari is yellowish, greenish or tawny in the dictionaries (in yajus 2 it is the green of leaves); Sāyaṇa reads harikeśa of Rudra as dark-haired, without grey. The translation follows Sāyaṇa; the word table gives both.

DCS (TS 4.5.2) annotates puṣṭānām as a neuter (‘of things that thrive’); Sāyaṇa takes it as masculine, men complete in good qualities. The genitive plural is the same in both genders; the word table follows Sāyaṇa.

vyakarana.note: Dative singular of the feminine i-stem heti, ‘missile, weapon’, with the ending -ai (hetyai; the alternative form is hetaye). Like the other datives it depends on namaḥ; bhavasya depends on it: ‘to the weapon of Bhava’.
jagat, originally the present participle of √gam (reduplicated), ‘moving’, used as a neuter noun, ‘what moves, the world’; genitive plural.

translation.literal: Homage to the weapon of Bhava; to the lord of the worlds homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the weapon of Bhava; homage to the lord of all that moves.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa’s comment on this yajus is missing from the transcription of the bhāṣya used here: the text breaks off after the word that introduces it, with the transcriber’s note that the commentary was not found, and the comment that follows (on the seventh yajus) is numbered as the sixth. The word meanings here therefore rest on the grammar and the dictionary. Bhava is one of Rudra’s names, by which the hymn salutes him again in the fifth anuvāka.

flags.note: No comment of Sāyaṇa on this yajus survives in the witness (sayana.json, N2: «अथ (अत्र टीकाभागः न लब्धः??)»), and the next comment is headed «अथ षष्ठं यजुराह— नमो रुद्रायेति», though it is the seventh yajus. The unit count (13) is Sāyaṇa’s own and is not affected.

samasa.meaning: he who protects with the bow stretched; Sāyaṇa’s analysis (ātata, ‘stretched’, + √av, ‘to protect’)

vyakarana.note: Dative singular of ātatāvin. ātata is the past participle of ā-√tan, ‘to stretch’ (the bow drawn). Sāyaṇa takes the rest from √av, ‘to protect’. Monier-Williams treats ātatāvin as the Taittirīya reading of ātatāyin, ‘having one’s bow drawn’.
Genitive plural of kṣetra; n becomes ṇ after the r of the same word (P. 8.4.1–2).

translation.literal: Homage to Rudra, the protector with the drawn [bow]; to the lord of the fields homage.
translation.readable: Homage to Rudra, who guards with his bow drawn; homage to the lord of the fields.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: ātatāvin is he who protects with the bow stretched («आततेन विस्तारितेन धनुषाऽवति रक्षतीत्याततावी»); homage is to that Rudra. The lord of the fields is the Rudra who protects them («क्षेत्राणां पालको यो रुद्रः»).

flags.note: ātatāvin: Monier-Williams (under ātatāyin) ‘having one’s bow drawn’, a possessive formation; Sāyaṇa derives the second part from √av, ‘who protects with the drawn bow’. The translation follows Sāyaṇa.
W1 marks the syllable tā of ātatāvine anudātta (आतता॒विने॒); W2 leaves it unmarked (रु॒द्राया॑तताविने॒). The text follows W1.

vyakarana.note: hantya is a gerundive of √han, ‘to slay’ (‘to be slain’), negated by a-. Dative singular. DCS divides the same way (a + hantya, gerundive).

translation.literal: Homage to the charioteer, to the one not to be slain; to the lord of the forests homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the charioteer whom none can slay; homage to the lord of the forests.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «सूतः सारथिः» — sūta is the charioteer — and «अहन्त्यो वैरिभिर्हन्तुमशक्यः», ahantya is one whom enemies cannot slay; homage is to Rudra in that form. The lord of the forests is the Rudra who protects them («यो वनानां पालकस्तस्मै रुद्राय नमोऽस्तु»).

vyakarana.note: sthapati is itself a compound with pati, ‘lord’: Monier-Williams explains it as ‘place-lord’ and notes that some derive it otherwise. Because its first member is not certain it is not analysed here. Being compounded, it has the ordinary i-stem dative sthapataye in Classical Sanskrit too.
Genitive plural of vṛkṣa; n becomes ṇ after ṣ in the same word (P. 8.4.1).

translation.literal: Homage to the red one, to the chief; to the lord of the trees homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the red one, the chief; homage to the lord of the trees.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «रोहितो लोहितवर्णः» — rohita is red in colour — and «स्थपतिः प्रभुः», the sthapati is the master; homage is to that Rudra. The lord of the trees is he who protects them («वृक्षाणां यः पालकस्तस्मै नमोऽस्तु»).

flags.note: The first member of sthapati is uncertain (Monier-Williams: ‘place-lord’, with other derivations recorded), so no samāsa analysis is given; Sāyaṇa glosses only the whole word.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: the mantrin is one skilled in weighing counsel in the king’s assembly («राजसभायां मन्त्रालोचनकुशलो मन्त्री»); he is vāṇija as the master of the merchants («वणिजां स्वामित्वेन वाणिजस्»). The kakṣa are the shrubs and the like that grow in the forest («वनगता गुल्मादयः कक्षाः»), and homage is to their protector.

samasa.meaning: he who spreads out the earth (Sāyaṇa; Monier-Williams gives the same analysis from Mahīdhara)

samasa.vigraha: वरिवः करोतीति वरिवस्कृत्, स एव वारिवस्कृतः
samasa.meaning: maker of varivas (room, relief; for Sāyaṇa, wealth), with a secondary vṛddhi derivative of the same meaning

vyakarana.note: Dative singular of the i-stem bhuvanti, a word of the Rudra litany analysed by Sāyaṇa as bhuvam (accusative of bhū, ‘earth’, kept in the compound) + tan, ‘to spread out’.

varivaskṛt, ‘making room, giving relief’ (Monier-Williams, Ṛgveda and Taittirīya), and from it, with vṛddhi of the first syllable and the same meaning, vārivaskṛta (Sāyaṇa: «वरिवस्कृत्स एव वारिवस्कृतः»). Dative singular.
Genitive plural of oṣadhi f., ‘plant, herb’, dependent on pataye. The stem is oṣadhi (Sāyaṇa: «ओषधीनां ग्राम्यारण्यानां»); the au of the text is vārivaskṛtāya + oṣadhīnām.

translation.literal: Homage to the one who spreads out the earth, to the maker of wealth; to the lord of the plants homage.
translation.readable: Homage to him who spreads out the earth and bestows wealth; homage to the lord of the plants.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: bhuvanti is he who spreads out the earth («भुवं तनोतीति»). varivas means wealth, its maker is varivaskṛt, and vārivaskṛta is the same («वरिवस्कृत्स एव वारिवस्कृतः»). The plants are those of the village and of the forest («ओषधीनां ग्राम्यारण्यानां»), and their lord is their protector.

flags.note: varivas is ‘room, free space, ease’ in Monier-Williams (‘wealth’ only from the Nighaṇṭu); Sāyaṇa takes it as wealth. The translation follows Sāyaṇa; the word table gives both.

DCS (TS 4.5.2) divides वारिवस्कृतायौषधीनाम् as vārivaskṛtāya + auṣadhīnām (lemma auṣadhī). The stem is oṣadhi, as Sāyaṇa reads it; the au is the vṛddhi of a + o at the junction. The padaccheda keeps ओषधीनाम्.

words.context: the verb astu, ‘be’, is understood: ‘homage [be] to …’ (Sāyaṇa: नमोऽस्तु)

words.gram: m. dat. sg. of the present participle of the causative of ā-√krand
words.meaning: to the one who makes [others] cry out; who roars at
words.context: Sāyaṇa: रोदयिता, he who makes the enemies weep

samasa.meaning: he whose cry is loud; inside the compound uccaiḥ becomes uccair before the voiced gh

vyakarana.note: The first member is the indeclinable uccaiḥ, ‘aloft, loudly’, used as an adjective of ghoṣa, ‘cry, noise’.

ā-√krand, ‘to cry out’; causative stem ā-krandaya-, present participle ā-krandayat, dative singular -ate. Monier-Williams gives the participle as ‘shouting at, roaring at’; Sāyaṇa takes the causative literally, ‘making [the enemies] weep’.
Genitive plural of the i-stem patti m., ‘one who goes on foot’, with the long ī of -īnām.

translation.literal: Homage to the one whose cry is loud, to the one who makes [the enemies] cry out; to the lord of the foot-soldiers homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the loud-crying one who makes his enemies weep; homage to the lord of the foot-soldiers.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: uccairghoṣa is he whose cry is raised high in time of battle («युद्धकाल उच्छ्रितो»…), and ākrandayat he who makes the enemies weep («रोदयिता»); homage is to that Rudra. The patti are the warriors who go on foot («पादचारिणो योधाः»), and homage is to their protector.

flags.note: ākrandayate: Monier-Williams ‘shouting at, roaring at’; Sāyaṇa ‘making the enemies weep’. The translation follows Sāyaṇa; the word table gives both.

words.context: the verb astu, ‘be’, is understood: ‘homage [be] to …’ (Sāyaṇa: नमोऽस्तु)
Sāyaṇa: he by whom the whole army is surrounded

words.gram: m. dat. sg. of the present participle of √dhāv (1st class, P.)
words.context: Sāyaṇa: running behind the fleeing armies of the enemy
Sāyaṇa: of the good who have taken refuge (सात्त्विकाः शरणागताः)
Sāyaṇa: पालकः, protector
the closing salutation of the yajus and of the anuvāka

sandhi.rule: visarga before k is written as the jihvāmūlīya ᳵ (P. 8.3.37)
final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra, written as the nasal of the next consonant’s class (m before p; P. 8.3.23, 8.4.59)

samasa.vigraha: कृत्स्नं सैन्यं वीतं वेष्टितं येन असौ कृत्स्नवीतः
samasa.meaning: he by whom the whole army is surrounded (Sāyaṇa); in Monier-Williams, ‘completely covered or mailed’

vyakarana.note: vīta is the past participle of √vye, ‘to cover, wrap’ (DCS: lemma vye). Sāyaṇa makes the compound a bahuvrīhi; the dictionary’s ‘completely covered’ takes it of Rudra himself.
√dhāv, ‘to run’, present participle dhāvat, dative singular -ate.
Genitive plural of the n-stem satvan, ‘warrior’ (Vedic). The anuvāka ends with namaḥ in its pausal form before the double danda.

translation.literal: Homage to the one by whom [the whole army] is surrounded, to the one who runs; to the lord of the warriors homage.
translation.readable: Homage to him who encircles the whole army and runs in pursuit; homage to the lord of the warriors.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: kṛtsnavīta is he by whom the whole army is surrounded («कृत्स्नं सैन्यं वीतं वेष्टितं येनासौ कृत्स्नवीतः»); dhāvat is he who runs after the fleeing («पलायमानानां») armies of the enemy, going behind them («पृष्ठतो गच्छन्»). He takes the satvan as the good who have taken refuge («सात्त्विकाः शरणागताः»), and homage is to their protector. So ends his comment on the second anuvāka.

flags.note: satvan is ‘warrior; pl. warriors, followers’ in Monier-Williams (and DCS: satvan); Sāyaṇa, whose text writes सत्त्वानः, glosses them as the sāttvika who have taken refuge. The translation keeps ‘warriors’; the traditional note gives his reading.
kṛtsnavīta: Monier-Williams ‘completely covered or mailed’ (of the god himself); Sāyaṇa a bahuvrīhi, ‘he by whom the whole army is surrounded’. The translation follows Sāyaṇa.
